lessons.title: Digestion and absorption in detail

objectives: Describe the action of the main digestive enzymes
Describe the role of bile and the pancreas
Explain how the small intestine is adapted for absorption
Describe the fate of absorbed nutrients
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Enzyme names and pH values are textbook-level; check against the syllabus diagrams.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Enzymes of digestion
blocks.md: **Salivary amylase** (mouth): starch to maltose. **Pepsin** (stomach, acid pH about 2): protein to shorter polypeptides. **Pancreatic amylase, proteases (trypsin) and lipase** (small intestine, near-neutral pH): starch, proteins and fats. **Brush-border enzymes** finish digestion: maltase (maltose to glucose), sucrase, lactase, peptidases. **Bile** (made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder) has no enzymes but **emulsifies** fat to give a larger surface for lipase and neutralises stomach acid.

blocks.title: Absorption
blocks.md: The small intestine is long with a lining folded into **villi** and microvilli, giving a very large surface area; thin walls and a rich blood supply (and a lacteal) speed absorption. Glucose and amino acids are absorbed into the blood (partly by active transport) and go to the liver; fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the lacteal (lymph) and reach the blood later. The large intestine absorbs water.

blocks.caption: A table of four digestive enzymes with substrates and products.
blocks.alt: Table: amylase starch to maltose, pepsin protein to polypeptides, lipase fats to fatty acids and glycerol, maltase maltose to glucose.

blocks.title: After absorption
blocks.md: The **liver** controls blood glucose (stores glycogen), deaminates excess amino acids (making urea), makes bile and proteins and stores some vitamins and minerals. Glucose is used for respiration, extra is stored as glycogen or fat. Amino acids build proteins; fatty acids are used for energy or stored in adipose tissue.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Bile does not digest fat chemically; it emulsifies it.
- Pepsin works in acid, trypsin in near-neutral conditions: the optimum pH differs.
- Lactose intolerance is a lack of lactase, not an allergy to milk protein (health matters for a professional).
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Chain
blocks.statement: Trace the digestion of starch to glucose.
steps: Salivary and pancreatic amylase break starch into maltose.
Maltase on the intestinal lining breaks maltose into glucose, which is absorbed.

blocks.title: Example 2 - pH
blocks.statement: Why does pepsin stop working in the small intestine?
steps: Pepsin's optimum is acidic pH; the small intestine is near neutral.
Bile and pancreatic juice raise the pH, so pepsin is inactive.

objectives: Describe bacteria, yeasts and moulds in food
Describe factors affecting microbial growth and the growth curve
Distinguish food infection from food intoxication
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Temperature and pH thresholds are widely used guidance values (about 5-60 degrees; pH 4.6) and must be checked. Doubling times are illustrative.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Microorganisms
blocks.md: **Bacteria** (single-celled, divide by binary fission), **yeasts** (single-celled fungi, ferment sugars to alcohol and carbon dioxide) and **moulds** (multicellular fungi with filaments; spoil bread, fruit and stored grains). Useful uses: yoghurt, cheese, bread, fermented foods; harmful uses: spoilage and disease.

blocks.title: Growth factors
blocks.md: **Temperature** (many pathogens grow roughly between 5 and 60 degrees Celsius), **moisture** (water available), **pH** (most bacteria prefer near neutral; below about 4.6 many are inhibited), **nutrients**, **oxygen** (aerobic, anaerobic, facultative) and **time**. A bacterial growth curve has **lag**, **log (exponential)**, **stationary** and **death** phases. In ideal conditions some bacteria divide about every 20 to 30 minutes, so N = N0 x 2^(t/g).

items.text: Death: nutrients used, wastes build up

blocks.caption: Four boxes listing the lag, log, stationary and death phases of bacterial growth.
blocks.alt: Flow of bacterial growth phases: lag, log, stationary, death.

blocks.title: Food-borne illness
blocks.md: **Infection**: living bacteria are swallowed and grow in the body (e.g. Salmonella). **Intoxication**: a toxin already formed in the food causes illness (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus toxin, Bacillus cereus on reheated rice). Water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid spread through unsafe water and poor sanitation. Moulds on groundnuts and maize can produce **aflatoxins**.

blocks.title: HACCP (outline)
blocks.md: **Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points** is a system that prevents hazards: identify hazards, find critical control points (e.g. cooking temperature), set critical limits, monitor, take corrective action, verify the system and keep records. It supports **good hygiene practice**, personal hygiene, cleaning and pest control.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Cooking does not remove toxins that are heat-stable.
- Bacteria are not killed by freezing; they only stop growing.
- HACCP is prevention, not only final inspection.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Growth
blocks.statement: A food has 100 bacteria per gram. They divide every 30 minutes. How many after 3 hours?

blocks.title: Example 2 - HACCP
blocks.statement: In a school canteen, which step could be a critical control point for chicken, and what could be the limit?
steps: Cooking is a point where germs can be killed.
Limit: the centre must reach a safe temperature (about 70 degrees Celsius or as set by the local authority) and be recorded.

objectives: Carry out the standard tests for starch, reducing sugar, protein, lipid and vitamin C
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Reagent concentrations, quantities and school-lab safety rules must be taken from the official practical guide and approved by a teacher.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Standard tests
blocks.md: **Starch**: iodine solution turns blue-black. **Reducing sugar**: heat with Benedict's solution; blue to green, yellow, orange, brick-red. **Protein**: biuret test; sodium hydroxide then dilute copper(II) sulfate; a violet (purple) colour. **Lipid**: emulsion test; shake the food with ethanol, then pour into water; a cloudy white emulsion. **Vitamin C**: DCPIP (blue) is decolourised.

blocks.title: Method and records
blocks.md: State the aim, apparatus, method, safety, results table and conclusion. Test a **control** (water, which should give a negative result) and known positive samples. Use the same volumes and same heating time. For vitamin C, count drops of juice needed to decolourise a fixed volume of DCPIP; **fewer drops** means **more** vitamin C.

blocks.caption: A table of four food tests and their positive results.
blocks.alt: Table: iodine test blue-black, Benedict's orange or brick-red, biuret violet, ethanol emulsion cloudy white.

blocks.title: Safety
blocks.md: Wear eye protection; use a water bath, not direct flame, for heating test tubes with Benedict's; hold test tubes at an angle and point them away from people; ethanol is flammable; wash hands; never taste in the laboratory; dispose of chemicals as taught.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Not comparing with a control.
- Changing the volumes between samples.
- Reading vitamin C results backwards.
- Following safety only if a teacher is watching.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Interpret
blocks.statement: Egg white gives violet with biuret and no change with iodine or Benedict's. What does it contain?
steps: No change with iodine and Benedict's shows no starch and no reducing sugar.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Vitamin C
blocks.statement: Juice A decolourises the DCPIP after 8 drops, juice B after 20 drops (same volume of DCPIP). Which has more vitamin C?
steps: Fewer drops are needed when the juice is richer in vitamin C.
Juice A needed fewer drops, so it has more vitamin C.
